proofs.trap: Consecutive integers: one of them must be even. Do not assume both are.

proofs.title: The product of two consecutive integers is even
proofs.given: n is an integer.
steps: Either n is even or n is odd
Every integer is even or odd
Case 1: n = 2k, so n(n + 1) = 2k(n + 1), which is even
In both cases n(n + 1) is even
proofs.idea: Split into cases by parity and show a factor of 2 appears in each.
proofs.deep: The same idea shows that the product of any k consecutive integers is divisible by k!.
proofs.trap: A proof by cases must cover EVERY case. Here there are only two.

proofs.title: The sum of three consecutive integers is divisible by 3
proofs.given: n is an integer. The three consecutive integers are n, n + 1, n + 2.
steps: n + 1 is an integer, so the sum is a multiple of 3
proofs.idea: Write the three numbers using one variable and add.
proofs.deep: The middle number n + 1 times 3 is the sum. The average of consecutive numbers is the middle one.
proofs.trap: Do not use three different letters. They would not be consecutive.

proofs.title: n³ − n is always divisible by 6
proofs.given: n is an integer.
steps: (n − 1)n(n + 1) is a product of three consecutive integers
One of three consecutive integers is a multiple of 3, and at least one is even
The product is divisible by 2 and by 3, and gcd(2, 3) = 1, so by 6
proofs.idea: Factor to reveal three consecutive integers, then count the factors of 2 and 3.
proofs.deep: The number 6 = 3! is the product of 1·2·3. This is the general rule for k consecutive integers.
proofs.trap: Divisible by 2 and 3 gives 6 only because 2 and 3 share no common factor.

proofs.title: The sum of the first n odd numbers is n²
proofs.given: The first n odd numbers are 1, 3, 5, …, 2n − 1.
steps: Pair the first term with the last: 1 + (2n − 1) = 2n
Pair the second with the second-to-last: 3 + (2n − 3) = 2n
Each of the n/2 pairs adds to 2n
Multiplication (number of pairs × sum of pair)
proofs.idea: Pair numbers from opposite ends so every pair has the same sum.
proofs.deep: A picture proof: add an L-shaped border of 2k − 1 squares to a k × k square to get a (k + 1) × (k + 1) square.
proofs.trap: Pairing works because the pairs sum to a constant. For odd n, the middle term is paired with itself and gives n, so the total is the same.

proofs.title: The sum 1 + 2 + … + n equals n(n + 1)/2
steps: Add the two equations term by term
proofs.idea: Add the sum to itself written backwards so each column adds to the same number.
proofs.deep: This is Gauss’s trick. The same method gives any arithmetic series: S = n(a₁ + aₙ)/2.
proofs.trap: There are n pairs, not n/2, when you add two copies of the sum. Then divide by 2.

proofs.title: The finite geometric series: 1 + r + … + rⁿ = (rⁿ⁺¹ − 1)/(r − 1)
proofs.given: r ≠ 1 and S = 1 + r + r² + … + rⁿ.
proofs.idea: Multiply by r and subtract; almost everything cancels.
proofs.deep: If |r| < 1, rⁿ⁺¹ goes to 0 and the sum tends to 1/(1 − r). This explains why 0.999… = 1.
proofs.trap: If r = 1 the division is by zero. In that case the sum is simply n + 1.

proofs.given: x = 0.999… (the 9s never stop).
proofs.idea: Multiply by 10 so the repeating tails line up and cancel.
proofs.deep: This works because 10x has the same tail of 9s as x. It also shows how to turn any repeating decimal into a fraction.
proofs.trap: There is no “last 9”, so the subtraction leaves exactly 9.

proofs.given: x = 0.272727… (the block 27 repeats).
steps: Multiply by 100 (the repeating block has 2 digits)
proofs.idea: Match the multiplier to the length of the repeating block.
proofs.deep: A block of n digits needs a multiplier of 10ⁿ. The denominator is always 99…9 before simplifying.
proofs.trap: Multiplying by 10 here would leave the tails misaligned.

proofs.title: Difference of squares: a² − b² = (a + b)(a − b)
proofs.given: a and b are real numbers.
steps: (a + b)(a − b) = a(a − b) + b(a − b)
proofs.idea: Expand the right side and watch the middle terms cancel.
proofs.deep: A picture proof: cut a square of side a with a b × b corner removed into a rectangle with sides a + b and a − b.
proofs.trap: It is a difference of squares. a² + b² cannot be factored over the real numbers.

proofs.title: Square of a binomial: (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b²
proofs.given: a and b are real numbers.
steps: Commutative property (ab = ba) and combine like terms
proofs.idea: Write the square as a product and expand.
proofs.deep: A picture proof: a square of side a + b contains squares a² and b² and two rectangles ab.
proofs.trap: (a + b)² is not a² + b². The middle term 2ab is always there.

proofs.title: Sum and difference of cubes
proofs.given: a and b are real numbers.
steps: (a − b)(a² + ab + b²) = a(a² + ab + b²) − b(a² + ab + b²)
= a³ + a²b + ab² − a²b − ab² − b³
proofs.idea: Expand the right-hand side; everything between a³ and b³ cancels.
proofs.deep: Replace b with −b to get a³ + b³ = (a + b)(a² − ab + b²).
proofs.trap: The middle factor has a plus sign for a difference of cubes and a minus sign for a sum. SOAP: Same, Opposite, Always Positive.

proofs.title: AM–GM: for non-negative a and b, (a + b)/2 ≥ √(ab)
proofs.given: a ≥ 0 and b ≥ 0.
proofs.idea: Start from something that must be true (a square is non-negative) and expand it.
proofs.deep: Equality holds exactly when a = b. For a fixed sum, the product is largest when the numbers are equal, so a square has the largest area for a given perimeter.
proofs.trap: Both numbers must be non-negative or the square root is undefined.

proofs.title: a² + b² ≥ 2ab for all real numbers
proofs.given: a and b are real numbers.
proofs.idea: Think of a square that must be non-negative.
proofs.deep: No sign assumption is needed here, unlike AM–GM. Equality when a = b.
proofs.trap: Do not divide by something that could be zero or negative.

proofs.title: Zero-product property
proofs.given: a and b are real numbers and ab = 0.
steps: Multiplicative inverse and identity; 0 times anything is 0
proofs.idea: Assume a is not zero, then use its reciprocal to isolate b.
proofs.deep: This is why factoring solves quadratics: (x − 2)(x + 3) = 0 means one factor is 0. It FAILS for “= 5”.
proofs.trap: Only use it when the product equals 0. (x − 2)(x + 3) = 6 does not mean x − 2 = 6.

proofs.title: Derivation of the quadratic formula
proofs.given: ax² + bx + c = 0 with a ≠ 0.
steps: Divide by a and subtract c/a
Factor the left side; combine fractions
proofs.idea: Complete the square on the general equation.
proofs.deep: The formula packages one method for every quadratic. The discriminant b² − 4ac tells you how many real roots there are.
proofs.trap: Add the same quantity to BOTH sides when completing the square.

proofs.title: The vertex of y = ax² + bx + c is at x = −b/(2a)
proofs.given: y = ax² + bx + c with a ≠ 0.
steps: Factor a from the first two terms
The extreme value occurs at x = −b/(2a)
Substitution (the squared term is smallest or largest there)
proofs.idea: Complete the square. The squared term is 0 only at the vertex.
proofs.deep: The parabola is symmetric about this line, which is also halfway between the roots (x₁ + x₂)/2.
proofs.trap: The sign of a decides whether the vertex is a minimum (a > 0) or a maximum (a < 0).

proofs.title: Sum and product of roots: x₁ + x₂ = −b/a and x₁x₂ = c/a
proofs.given: ax² + bx + c = 0 has roots x₁ and x₂.
steps: ax² + bx + c = a(x − x₁)(x − x₂)
a(x − x₁)(x − x₂) = a(x² − (x₁ + x₂)x + x₁x₂)
ax² + bx + c = ax² − a(x₁ + x₂)x + a·x₁x₂
proofs.idea: Write the quadratic as a product of its roots and match the coefficients.
proofs.deep: These relationships let you check solutions fast and build a quadratic from its roots.
proofs.trap: Notice the minus sign in −b/a.

proofs.title: The discriminant tells how many real roots a quadratic has
proofs.given: ax² + bx + c = 0 with a ≠ 0 and D = b² − 4ac.
proofs.prove: D > 0: two real roots; D = 0: one; D < 0: none
steps: If D > 0, √D is a positive real number, so ± gives two different values
If D = 0, √D = 0, so both values equal −b/(2a)
If D < 0, √D is not a real number, so there are no real solutions
Square roots of negatives are not real
proofs.idea: Look only at the number under the square root.
proofs.deep: Graphically: D > 0 means the parabola crosses the x-axis twice, D = 0 touches it once, D < 0 misses it.
proofs.trap: D < 0 means no REAL roots. There are complex roots, but only the real number line is graphed.

proofs.title: a^m · a^n = a^(m + n)
proofs.given: a is a real number and m, n are positive integers.
steps: a^m · a^n has m + n factors of a
proofs.idea: Count the number of copies of a being multiplied.
proofs.deep: This law is why logarithms turn multiplication into addition.
proofs.trap: Add the exponents when you multiply. Multiply the exponents when you raise a power to a power.

proofs.title: (a^m)^n = a^(mn)
proofs.given: a is a real number and m, n are positive integers.
steps: Each a^m has m factors of a
The product has n groups of m factors, so mn factors of a
proofs.idea: Think of n groups of m copies each.
proofs.deep: This is different from a^(m^n). Powers stack from the top down.
proofs.trap: (a^m)^n multiplies exponents; a^m · a^n adds them. Do not mix these.

proofs.title: a⁰ = 1 for a ≠ 0
steps: Product law for exponents (keep it valid for exponent 0)
proofs.idea: Decide what a⁰ must be so the product law still works.
proofs.deep: This is a definition forced by consistency. 0⁰ is left undefined because the pattern breaks.
proofs.trap: The base must not be 0, or you would divide by zero.

proofs.title: a^(−n) = 1/aⁿ for a ≠ 0
proofs.given: a ≠ 0 and n is a positive integer.
proofs.idea: Choose the meaning of a negative exponent that keeps the product law true.
proofs.deep: A negative exponent means reciprocal, not a negative number: 2⁻³ = 1/8, not −8.
proofs.trap: Negative exponent is not negative result.

proofs.title: √(ab) = √a · √b for a, b ≥ 0
proofs.given: a ≥ 0 and b ≥ 0.
steps: √a · √b is non-negative and its square is ab
Product of non-negative numbers is non-negative
Definition of the principal square root
proofs.idea: Show that √a · √b is the non-negative number whose square is ab.
proofs.deep: This is the rule used to simplify radicals: √72 = √36 · √2 = 6√2.
proofs.trap: This rule does NOT work for sums: √(a + b) ≠ √a + √b.

proofs.title: √(x²) = |x|
proofs.given: x is any real number.
steps: If x ≥ 0 then x² has principal root x
Algebra: the square of a negative
proofs.idea: The radical symbol always gives the non-negative root, so negative x must be flipped.
proofs.deep: This is why solving x² = 9 gives x = ±3 but √9 = 3.
proofs.trap: Do not write √(x²) = x without knowing that x ≥ 0.

proofs.title: Rationalizing: 1/(√a + √b) = (√a − √b)/(a − b)
proofs.idea: Use the conjugate so the denominator becomes a difference of squares.
proofs.deep: The conjugate has the same terms with the opposite sign in the middle.
proofs.trap: Multiply BOTH the numerator and the denominator.

proofs.title: √3 is irrational (indirect proof)
proofs.given: √3 is a positive real number.
steps: Assume √3 = p/q where p, q are positive integers with no common factor
Square both sides and clear fractions
3 is prime: if a prime divides a square it divides the base
Division and the same prime argument
3 divides both p and q, contradicting “no common factor”
proofs.idea: Assume it is a fraction in lowest terms, then show that 3 divides both top and bottom.
proofs.deep: The same proof works for √p for every prime p. It fails for √4 because 4 is not prime.
proofs.trap: The step “3 | p² implies 3 | p” needs 3 to be prime. It would be false for 4 | 2².

proofs.title: A rational plus an irrational is irrational
proofs.given: r is rational and s is irrational.
steps: Assume r + s = t where t is rational
The difference of two rationals is rational
This contradicts that s is irrational, so r + s is irrational
proofs.idea: Suppose the sum is rational, and solve for the irrational number.
proofs.deep: Same idea: a nonzero rational times an irrational is irrational. Two irrationals can add to a rational: √2 + (−√2) = 0.
proofs.trap: The sum of two irrationals can be rational. Do not generalise.

proofs.title: A nonzero rational times an irrational is irrational
proofs.given: r ≠ 0 is rational and s is irrational.
steps: Assume rs = t with t rational
The quotient of rationals (with nonzero divisor) is rational
Contradiction with s irrational, so rs is irrational
proofs.idea: Assume the product is rational, then divide by r.
proofs.deep: r = 0 fails: 0 × √2 = 0, which is rational.
proofs.trap: The condition r ≠ 0 is what lets you divide.

proofs.title: The average of two numbers lies between them
proofs.given: a < b.
steps: a + b < b + b, so (a + b)/2 < b
Same steps on the other side
proofs.idea: Add a or b to both sides of a < b and divide by 2.
proofs.deep: This shows there is no “next” real number after a. Between any two reals there is always another.
proofs.trap: Dividing by a positive number keeps the direction. Dividing by a negative would flip it.

proofs.title: A two-digit number minus its reverse is a multiple of 9
proofs.given: A two-digit number has tens digit a and ones digit b, so its value is 10a + b.
steps: The number is 10a + b and the reversed number is 10b + a
a − b is an integer, so the difference is a multiple of 9
proofs.idea: Write the digits using place value and subtract.
proofs.deep: The digit sum rule for 9 works because 10 ≡ 1 (mod 9), so every digit counts just once.
proofs.trap: Place value matters: the tens digit counts as 10a, not a.

proofs.title: A number is divisible by 3 if its digit sum is (three-digit case)
proofs.given: N = 100a + 10b + c with digits a, b, c.
proofs.prove: 3 | N if and only if 3 | (a + b + c)
steps: N is divisible by 3 exactly when a + b + c is divisible by 3
The first part is always a multiple of 3
proofs.idea: Split off the multiples of 9 (or 3), so what remains is the digit sum.
proofs.deep: The same proof gives the rule for 9. It works because 10, 100, … are each one more than a multiple of 9.
proofs.trap: It is an “if and only if”: both directions follow from the same equation.

proofs.title: Pigeonhole: among any 13 people, two share a birth month
proofs.given: 13 people, 12 months.
proofs.prove: At least two people share a birth month
steps: Assume everyone has a different birth month
So two people share a birth month
proofs.idea: Assume no month repeats and count how many months you would need.
proofs.deep: The pigeonhole principle: n + 1 objects in n boxes force a box with two. It proves surprising results with no calculation.
proofs.trap: The principle says two people share a month, not which two.

proofs.title: Point-slope form: y − y₁ = m(x − x₁)
proofs.given: A line has slope m and passes through (x₁, y₁). (x, y) is any other point on it.
proofs.idea: Write the slope between the fixed point and a general point.
proofs.deep: The point (x₁, y₁) also satisfies the equation, because both sides are 0.
proofs.trap: The signs inside the parentheses are opposite to the coordinates: (x − x₁), not (x + x₁).

proofs.title: Elimination keeps the solution of a system
proofs.given: x = p and y = q solve both a₁x + b₁y = c₁ and a₂x + b₂y = c₂.
proofs.prove: x = p and y = q also solve their sum (a₁ + a₂)x + (b₁ + b₂)y = c₁ + c₂
steps: a₁p + b₁q = c₁ and a₂p + b₂q = c₂
proofs.idea: Add true equations. The result is still true for the same numbers.
proofs.deep: The same works for multiplying an equation by a nonzero number. These two moves never lose the solution.
proofs.trap: Multiplying by 0 would destroy information. The multiplier must be nonzero.

proofs.title: The sum of two consecutive triangular numbers is a perfect square
proofs.idea: Write both triangular numbers with the formula and factor out the common part.
proofs.deep: A picture: put two staircases of dots together to make a square.
proofs.trap: T(n − 1) uses n − 1 in place of n, so its formula is (n − 1)n/2.

lessons.title: Undo, in reverse · Variables on both sides

cards.t: To solve an equation, undo what was done to x, in reverse order. Whatever you do to one side, do to the other.

lab.hook: Solve 2x + 3 = 11 by doing the same thing to both sides.
lab.take: Whatever you do to one side, do to the other.

cards.t: Move the x terms to one side and the numbers to the other. Then divide by the coefficient.

lab.hook: Where do the two lines meet? That x solves the equation.

cards.t: Multiply the number outside the parentheses by EVERY term inside. Then solve like normal.

lessons.title: Fractions in equations · Flip the sign

cards.t: Multiply every term by the denominator to clear the fraction. That keeps the equation balanced.
In an inequality, multiplying or dividing by a NEGATIVE flips the sign. Adding and subtracting never flips it.
Treat the other letters like numbers and undo operations in reverse. Formulas work the same way.
Slope tells how steep a line is: rise over run. Up-right is positive; down-right is negative.

lab.hook: Slope is rise over run. Change it and watch the steepness.
lab.out: Rise {m} for every 1 across. Positive goes up, negative goes down.

pre.q: Which line is steeper: slope 3 or slope 1?
pre.why: A bigger slope rises more for each step across.

cards.t: In y = mx + b, m is the slope and b is where the line crosses the y-axis.

lab.hook: y = mx + b: m tilts the line, b lifts it.
lab.out: y = {m}x + {b}. It crosses the y-axis at {b}.

cards.h: Make a line from a point
cards.t: Use the slope and a point to find b: plug x and y into y = mx + b, then solve for b.
Parallel lines have the same slope. Perpendicular slopes multiply to −1 (negative reciprocals).
Ax + By = C. To graph it, find the x- and y-intercepts by setting the other variable to 0.
In a word problem, slope is the rate (per hour, per item) and b is the starting amount.
A solution of a system is the point that makes BOTH equations true. On a graph it is where the lines cross.

lab.hook: A solution to a system is where the lines cross.
lab.out: The solution is the crossing point.

cards.t: Solve one equation for a letter, then plug that into the other equation. Best when a letter is already alone.
Add or subtract the equations so a letter cancels. Multiply an equation first if needed.

lessons.title: No or infinite solutions · Check your answer

cards.t: Parallel lines (same slope, different b) give NO solution. Same line gives infinitely many.
Plug your (x, y) into BOTH original equations. If both work, you are done.

lessons.title: Multiply, same base · Power of a power

cards.t: When multiplying powers with the same base, ADD the exponents.

lab.hook: Same base: add the exponents.

cards.t: For (xᵃ)ᵇ, MULTIPLY the exponents. Also raise every factor inside the parentheses.
When dividing, SUBTRACT the exponents (top minus bottom).
Anything (not 0) to the 0 is 1. A negative exponent means flip to the other side of the fraction.
Write a number as a × 10ⁿ with 1 ≤ a < 10. Moving the decimal left makes n bigger.

lessons.title: Factor out the GCF · Trinomials x² + bx + c

cards.t: Find the biggest number and letters shared by every term and pull them out. Always do this first.
Find two numbers that multiply to c and add to b. They go in the two parentheses.

lab.hook: Factors show where the parabola crosses the x-axis.

cards.t: a² − b² always factors into (a − b)(a + b). There must be a minus sign between two squares.
For ax² + bx + c, try the product a·c and split the middle term, then group.
If a product equals 0, one factor must be 0. Set each factor equal to 0 and solve.
√a asks: what number times itself gives a? Perfect squares: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, 64, 81, 100.

lab.hook: A square root finds the side of a square from its area.

cards.t: Pull out the biggest perfect square factor. √72 = √36 · √2 = 6√2.
√a · √b = √(ab). You can also split a root of a fraction into top and bottom.
Only LIKE radicals combine, just like like terms. Simplify first.
If a root is left in the denominator, multiply top and bottom by that root.
f(x) is the output for input x. To find f(3), replace every x with 3 and calculate.
The graph of y = ax² + bx + c is a parabola. If a > 0 it opens up; if a < 0, down.

lab.hook: Every parabola has the same shape; a squeezes it or flips it.
lab.out: a = {a}. Positive opens up, negative opens down.

cards.t: The vertex is the turning point. Its x-coordinate is −b/(2a). Plug in to get y.

lab.hook: The vertex is the turning point.

cards.t: Move everything to one side, factor, set each factor to 0.
When factoring fails, use the formula. The discriminant b² − 4ac tells how many real solutions.
Repeated percent change uses A = P(1 + r)ⁿ. Decay uses (1 − r).
Arithmetic adds the same number each time; geometric multiplies by the same number.
|x| is the distance from 0. |x − 3| = 5 means x is 5 away from 3, so two answers.

lessons.title: Point, line, plane · Segment and ray

cards.t: A point is a location. A line goes on forever in two directions. A plane is a flat surface that goes on forever.
A segment has two endpoints. A ray has one endpoint and goes on forever. Name a ray with its endpoint first.
An angle has a vertex and two sides. Acute < 90°, right = 90°, obtuse between 90° and 180°, straight = 180°.
Complementary add to 90°. Supplementary add to 180°. A linear pair is two adjacent angles that make a straight line.

lab.hook: Angles that sit on a straight line add to 180°.

cards.t: When two lines cross, the angles directly across from each other are equal.
A midpoint splits a segment into two equal parts. A bisector splits a segment or angle in half.
Reflexive: a = a. Symmetric: if a = b then b = a. Transitive: if a = b and b = c then a = c. Substitution lets you swap equals.
'If p, then q.' p is the hypothesis and q is the conclusion. A statement is true only if it can never fail.
Converse: swap p and q. Inverse: negate both. Contrapositive: swap AND negate. Only the contrapositive always matches the original.
One example that makes the hypothesis true and the conclusion false proves a statement false.
Inductive finds a pattern from examples and may be wrong. Deductive uses facts to reach a sure conclusion, like in a proof.
Each statement needs a reason: given, definition, postulate or theorem. Start with the givens; finish with what you prove.
Assume the opposite of what you want. Show it leads to a contradiction. Then the original must be true.

lessons.title: Parallel lines and a transversal · Same-side interior

cards.t: A transversal crosses two lines and makes 8 angles. With parallel lines, corresponding, alternate interior and alternate exterior angles are EQUAL.
Same-side interior angles between parallel lines add to 180°. Z shape means equal, C shape means supplementary.
The converses work: if corresponding or alternate interior angles are equal, the lines are parallel.

lessons.title: Angle sum in a triangle · Polygon angles

cards.t: The three angles of a triangle always add to 180°. An exterior angle equals the sum of the two remote interior angles.

lab.hook: Angles in any triangle always add to 180°.

pre.q: A triangle has angles 60° and 50°. The third angle is…

cards.t: Interior angle sum = (n − 2) × 180°. Exterior angles of any convex polygon add to 360°.

lab.hook: More sides, more angle total.
lab.note: A {n}-sided shape has angles totalling {=(n-2)*180|0}°. Each regular angle: {=(n-2)*180/n|1}°.

cards.t: A regular polygon has equal sides and equal angles. Each exterior angle = 360° ÷ n.

lessons.title: Congruent triangles · Four ways to prove it

cards.t: Congruent triangles are the same shape AND size. Matching parts are called corresponding parts.
SSS, SAS, ASA and AAS prove congruence. For right triangles, HL works. AAA and SSA do NOT.
After you prove triangles congruent, ALL their matching parts are congruent. This is how you prove segments or angles equal.
Equal sides have equal angles opposite them, and the other way around. The bisector of the vertex angle is also a median and an altitude.
A median goes to a midpoint, an altitude is perpendicular, an angle bisector splits an angle. The medians meet at the centroid.
Any two sides add to MORE than the third. The longest side is opposite the largest angle.
Perpendicular bisectors meet at the circumcenter; angle bisectors at the incenter; altitudes at the orthocenter.
Opposite sides are parallel and equal, opposite angles are equal, consecutive angles add to 180°, diagonals bisect each other.
Show ONE of: both pairs of opposite sides equal, one pair both parallel and equal, or diagonals bisect each other.
A parallelogram with four right angles. Its diagonals are equal.
A parallelogram with four equal sides. Its diagonals are perpendicular and bisect the angles.
A square is both a rectangle and a rhombus, so it has every one of those properties.
One pair of parallel sides (bases). The midsegment is parallel to the bases and equals their average.
Two pairs of equal adjacent sides. One diagonal is the perpendicular bisector of the other.
A ratio compares two numbers. A proportion says two ratios are equal. Cross-multiply to solve.
Same shape, different size. Corresponding angles are equal and corresponding sides are in the same ratio (the scale factor).
AA is enough. Also SAS∼ (two sides in proportion, included angle equal) and SSS∼ (all three sides in proportion).
A line parallel to one side of a triangle cuts the other two sides in proportion.
An angle bisector in a triangle divides the opposite side in the same ratio as the two sides next to it.
If the scale factor is k, perimeters scale by k and areas scale by k². Volumes scale by k³.

lab.hook: Scale a shape by k. Perimeter scales by k, area by k².

cards.t: In a right triangle, the legs squared add to the hypotenuse squared. The hypotenuse is opposite the right angle.

lab.hook: Legs a and b make a right triangle. Find the long side.

pre.q: Legs 3 and 4. The long side is…

cards.t: Whole-number triples show up often: 3-4-5, 5-12-13, 8-15-17, 7-24-25. Multiples work too.
The legs are equal and the hypotenuse is leg × √2.
Short leg x, long leg x√3, hypotenuse 2x.
In a right triangle, the altitude to the hypotenuse is the geometric mean of the two pieces. Each leg is the geometric mean of the hypotenuse and its adjacent piece.
SOH-CAH-TOA: sin = opp/hyp, cos = adj/hyp, tan = opp/adj. Label sides from the angle you are using.

lab.hook: Resize the triangle, change the angle, watch the ratios.

cards.t: Both angles are measured from the horizontal. They make alternate interior angles, so they are equal.

lessons.title: Circle vocabulary · Central angles and arcs

cards.t: Radius: center to the circle. Chord: two points on the circle. Diameter: chord through the center. Tangent: touches once. Secant: cuts twice.
A central angle has the same measure as its arc. A full circle is 360°.
An inscribed angle is HALF its intercepted arc. An angle in a semicircle is 90°.

lab.hook: The center angle is twice the angle on the edge.

lessons.title: Tangents · Angles with chords and secants

cards.t: A tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of touching. Two tangents from one outside point are equal.
Inside the circle: half the SUM of the arcs. Outside: half the DIFFERENCE of the arcs.
Two chords: part × part = part × part. Tangent: (tangent)² = whole secant × outside part.

lessons.title: The tools · Copy a segment or angle

cards.t: Classic constructions use only a compass and straightedge. The compass copies equal lengths.
Set the compass to the length and mark it off. For an angle, copy the arc and the chord that cuts it.
Arcs from both ends with equal radii cross at two points. The line through them is the perpendicular bisector.

lessons.title: Perpendicular and parallel · What is a locus?

cards.t: Use equal arcs to make a perpendicular from a point. Copying a corresponding angle makes a parallel line.
A locus is ALL points that satisfy a rule. Equidistant from two points: a perpendicular bisector. At distance r from a point: a circle.
To satisfy two rules, draw each locus and mark where they cross. Count the intersections.
Rectangle: length × width. Parallelogram: base × height, where height is perpendicular to the base.
A triangle is half of a parallelogram. Use any side as the base with its matching height.

lab.hook: A triangle is half of a rectangle.

cards.t: Average the two bases and multiply by the height.
Area = ½ × apothem × perimeter. The apothem goes from the center to the middle of a side.
Circumference = 2πr. Area = πr². Keep π in your answer for an exact value.

lab.hook: Circle area grows with radius squared.

cards.t: A sector is a fraction of the circle: angle/360. Multiply that fraction by the area or circumference.
If lengths scale by k, area scales by k².

lessons.title: Prisms and cylinders · Pyramids and cones

cards.t: Volume = base area × height. Lateral area is the sides only; total surface area adds the bases.
Volume is one third of a prism or cylinder with the same base and height.
Surface area 4πr². Volume (4/3)πr³.

lessons.title: Lateral and total area · Similar solids

cards.t: Cylinder lateral area = 2πrh. Total area adds two circles: 2πr² + 2πrh.
With scale factor k, surface areas scale by k² and volumes by k³.
Pyramids and cones use the slant height for lateral area. Find it with the Pythagorean theorem.
The distance between two points comes from the Pythagorean theorem.

lab.hook: Distance is the Pythagorean theorem on the grid.

cards.t: Average the x's and average the y's.
Rise over run. Parallel lines have equal slopes. Perpendicular lines have slopes that multiply to −1.
Center (h, k), radius r. Note the signs: the center's coordinates are subtracted.
Place a figure on axes with smart coordinates (a vertex at the origin). Use distance, slope or midpoint to prove properties.
Check side lengths and slopes. Equal and parallel opposite sides → parallelogram. Add right angles → rectangle.
Translations, reflections and rotations keep size and shape. A dilation keeps shape but changes size.
Slide every point the same way. Add the shift to each coordinate.
Flip over a line. Over the x-axis: (x, −y). Over the y-axis: (−x, y). Over y = x: (y, x).
Turn about a point. About the origin: 90° → (−y, x), 180° → (−x, −y), 270° → (y, −x).
A figure has line symmetry if a flip maps it onto itself. It has rotational symmetry if a turn less than 360° maps it onto itself.
A dilation multiplies coordinates by the scale factor k. Doing transformations one after another is a composition.

lab.hook: A dilation scales every length by the same factor.
